title: How Braille Works
summary: Josh and Chuck, with guest producer Matt Frederick, explain how Braille works. They cover Louis Braille's childhood blinding and his development of Braille from Charles Barbier's night writing, the competing tactile codes (including Valentin Haüy's raised Latin letters), the six-dot cell and its 63 combinations, uncontracted (Grade 1) versus contracted (Grade 2) Braille, reading and writing direction, Braille writers and refreshable displays, country-specific Braille codes (UK, Chinese, Hebrew, Tibetan, music, math, computer Braille), the debate over screen readers versus Braille literacy, reading speeds, and the US paper currency being the same size for every denomination, with a pocket Braille embosser suggested as a fix. The episode opens with personal banter about Guatemala and hepatitis shots and ends with a listener email from a young listener, Lucy, in Canada.

segments.title: Opening banter and Guatemala trip
segments.summary: Hosts discuss being in Guatemala, hepatitis shots, Josh feeling sick, and guest producer Matt Frederick's introduction, with off-topic banter about bands and King of the Hill.

segments.title: Louis Braille's blinding and early life
segments.summary: Louis Braille was blinded as a three-year-old by an awl from his father's leather shop, then lost sight in his other eye to sympathetic ophthalmia.

segments.title: Night writing and Braille's invention
segments.summary: Charles Barbier's night writing for soldiers inspired Braille, who as a teen simplified it into his own dot-based system, publishing his first Braille book by age twenty. Braille was slow to catch on, partly because of competing codes and bulky books.

segments.title: Competing tactile alphabets and Gutenberg comparison
segments.summary: Valentin Haüy's raised Latin-style tactile alphabet is described as an alternative, and Braille is compared to Gutenberg for making literacy possible for the blind. Bulky Braille books, such as the Harry Potter series, are noted.

segments.title: The six-dot Braille cell
segments.summary: Braille is built on a cell two dots wide and three dots tall, giving 63 combinations that cover letters, punctuation, contractions, numbers, and symbols. The number sign and capital sign are explained.

segments.title: Brain imaging and Braille reading
segments.summary: The hosts discuss fMRI studies showing the visual cortex activating during Braille reading, with theories about repurposed visual areas and language centers. They joke about the dead salmon fMRI study and express skepticism.

segments.title: Uncontracted versus contracted Braille
segments.summary: Grade 1 Braille spells out every word letter by letter, while Grade 2 contracts common letter groups and words. Debate exists over whether learners need uncontracted Braille first, and ATM keypads are mentioned as uncontracted examples.

segments.title: Writing Braille and devices
segments.summary: Braille is written right to left so it reads correctly when the page is flipped. Methods include a stylus, Braille writers with six keys, QWERTY keyboards attached to Braille printers, and refreshable tactile displays using pins, including a NASA-linked artificial muscle idea.

segments.title: Screen readers, audio books, and reading speed
segments.summary: Screen readers and audio books are discussed, including a critic who says they make blind people lazy. Reading speeds compare Braille readers at one to two hundred words per minute with eighth graders and college students.

segments.title: Braille codes around the world and US currency
segments.summary: Braille varies by country and by subject, including UK, Chinese, Hebrew, music, math, and computer Braille. Tibetan Braille was created by Sebrie Ten Berkin. The hosts also discuss US paper currency being identical in size across denominations and a pocket embosser that marks bills.
